definition: Sublime means so grand, beautiful, or excellent that it inspires awe — lofty greatness that rises beyond the ordinary.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word sublime. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know sublime should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The cellist's final encore was so sublime that the hall sat silent for three full seconds before the applause broke.
Impressive is weaker than sublime: an impressive view earns admiration and a photo, while a sublime one overwhelms you with awe that words can't reach.
Transcendent is stronger than sublime: the sublime fills you with awe at something vast, while the transcendent seems to leave the ordinary world behind entirely.

Majestic means grand, stately, and dignified in appearance — a majestic mountain or procession commands respect. Sublime goes to what the grandeur does to you: beauty or greatness so overwhelming it inspires awe and stops words.

Glorious means magnificently splendid and delightful — a glorious afternoon dazzles and pleases. Sublime runs deeper and quieter: instead of delighting you, it fills you with awe, as if you had brushed against something beyond the ordinary world.

Sublime is the top shelf of praise: use it when something inspires actual awe, and let majestic cover stately grandeur and glorious cover splendid delight.
It aims higher than beautiful — a beach can be beautiful while the storm rolling over it is sublime.
Food writers borrow it for a perfect dish ('a sublime risotto'); that is deliberate hyperbole, promoting dinner to the rank of a canyon at dawn.

Mara had seen a thousand photographs of the canyon, so she expected to feel prepared.
When the trail bent and the ground fell away into a mile of layered stone and light, her thoughts simply stopped, and the wind seemed to stop with them.
She had planned to take a picture; her phone stayed in her pocket.
She had planned to say something; nothing came.
Later she tried to explain it to her brother.
'Pretty is the wrong word,' she said.
'Beautiful is the wrong word.
It was sublime — it made me feel small and lucky at the same time.' The photographs, she decided, had shown her the canyon's shape but nothing of its power.
